curriculum.lesson_evidence: Sculpture is art in three dimensions: it has height, width and depth. Mass is the solid volume; negative space is the empty air around and through the form. Viewers can often walk around a sculpture, so every angle matters. Sketch front and side views before building.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Explain mass versus negative space using a chair as an example, and say why sculptors check more than one view.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Seat and legs are mass; gaps between legs are negative space. Other views stop the back looking unfinished.'

WATCH FOR
Decorating only the front face like a flat picture. Sculpture needs all-around thinking.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Draw front and side plans for a small sculpture idea. Label mass and one negative space, then build a quick foil or clay maquette.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.explain:
Sculpture is art in three dimensions: it has height, width and depth. Mass is the solid volume; negative space is the empty air around and through the form. Viewers can often walk around a sculpture, so every angle matters. Sketch front and side views before building.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.
